intro: Ichinohe maps one tree: the Wisteria of Fujishima, one of only eight vine-form trees ever given Japan's National Natural Monument status and the northernmost of them. Felled once by a typhoon and grown back on a steel trellis, it is tended today partly by schoolchildren from the elementary school next door and celebrated every May with a festival and night illumination. Published alone here because the tree itself is the destination, not because Ichinohe's research is finished.

question_meta: Ichinohe's oldest and only mapped tree is the Wisteria of Fujishima, one of Japan's eight National Natural Monument vine trees, free near Kozuya Station.
question_answer: Ichinohe's only mapped tree, and its oldest, is the Wisteria of Fujishima (Wisteria floribunda, Noda wisteria), a National Natural Monument several hundred years old, standing beside Kozuya Elementary School in Ichinohe, Iwate Prefecture.
question_context: Seven wisteria and one other vine have ever been given Japan's National Natural Monument status, and this is the northernmost of them, designated in 1938. The name Fujishima, wisteria island, comes from a moat that once ran on three sides. At designation it was reportedly the largest wisteria in Japan, but a 1954 typhoon felled its main stem, and it has grown supported on a steel trellis since; a 1995 reference records the trunk as internally rotted and split into seven pieces, though the wood under the bark is healthy and its overall vigour is good. A 1969 survey put the root circumference at 3.6 metres, other accounts round to 3.3 or 4, and its growth is said to reach past 20 metres. Its age is given only loosely, several hundred years, one account saying over 400, repeated here as vaguely as given. Schoolchildren next door take part in its conservation, a 2022 newspaper report found it in good bloom that May, and every year on the last Sunday of May the town holds a Wisteria Festival with night illumination. Free, on a signposted site with a small Benzaiten shrine at its base.

trees.story:
Seven wisteria and one other vine have ever been given Japan's National Natural Monument status, the country's highest tier of tree protection, and this is the northernmost of them. The name Fujishima, wisteria island, comes from a moat that used to run on three sides of the site, before it was filled in.

At its 1938 designation this was reportedly the largest wisteria in Japan. It has not had an easy run since. A 1954 typhoon felled its main stem, and it has grown supported on a steel trellis ever since; a 1995 reference book records the trunk as internally rotted and split into seven separate pieces, though the wood just under the bark is described as healthy and the tree's overall vigour as good.

Sources vary on its exact size, which is itself evidence of how hard this tree is to measure: a 1969 survey put the root circumference at 3.6 metres, other accounts round to 3.3 or 4, and its supported growth is said to reach past 20 metres. Its age gets the same treatment, several hundred years, one account says over 400, repeated here as loosely as the sources give it.

What is certain is that it is tended rather than merely preserved. Schoolchildren from the elementary school next door take part in its conservation programme, a 2022 newspaper report found it in good bloom that May, and every year on the last Sunday of May the town holds a Wisteria Festival with night illumination beneath it.
